# Selection — TRD §15 row 12: account-credential and slot-verifier construction

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-20
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 12 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol) — see §9, which answers the open question about
which review should hold it
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.9, §13.2, §13.4, §13.10, §6.5, §16.1 · PRD §6.7, §6.11, §7.6 ·
**Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.1
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/account-credential.json`](../../test/vectors/account-credential.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-account-credential-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-account-credential-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 1](./row-1-algorithm-suite.md) selects the primitives and the agility rule this row has to
bend once; [row 13](./row-13-device-lock.md) was expected to share this row's threat model and turns out to
share only half of it; [row 14](./row-14-recovery-code.md) §5 selects the bound challenge reused here;
[row 3](./row-3-record-format.md) supplies the rule about what a structured clone lets a reader trust;
[row 9](./row-9-chain-head-discovery.md) supplies the shape of the isolating negative.

---

## The selection

```
The account credential

  A WebAuthn discoverable credential (a passkey) on the account service's RP ID,
  created at account creation. Asymmetric: the service stores public material
  and holds no verifier secret.

  pubKeyCredParams, fixed and ordered, part of the carrier version:
      -8  Ed25519   preferred; already row 1's signature primitive
      -7  ES256     accepted; the algorithm most authenticators actually offer
  RS256 is not offered. Both accepted algorithms verify in WebCrypto, so the
  offline verifier needs no polyfill.

  No stretching, no KDF, no password. There is no secret in the profile.

The slot binding — one per credential, service-signed, in the slot index (§6.5)

  SlotBinding = { v: 1, account_id, principal_id, rp_id, epoch,
                  cred_id, public_key, sig }

    public_key   SubjectPublicKeyInfo, as PublicKeyCredential.getPublicKey()
                 returns it. Matched against a compiled-in set of two prefixes.
                 The algorithm is inside these bytes; there is no `alg` field.

    sig          Ed25519 by the authorization key of `epoch` (§13.5), over

      LP("done/slotbind/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(account_id) || LP(principal_id)
      || LP(rp_id) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(cred_id) || LP(hex public_key)

The unlock challenge — bound to the operation, not to a clock

  challenge = SHA-256( LP("done/slotunlock/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(principal_id)
                       || LP(cred_id) || LP(hex nonce) )

  nonce = 32 fresh random bytes per attempt.

Verification, offline, in this order

  1. sig verifies over the message above, under the epoch's authorization key.
  2. The returned credential id is the one this binding names.
  3. clientDataJSON: parsed, never rebuilt. type == "webauthn.get";
     origin == this origin; challenge == the one just minted;
     crossOrigin != true; topOrigin absent. (S0-1)
  4. authenticatorData: rpIdHash == SHA-256(rp_id); UP set; UV set.
     signCount is read and ignored.
  5. The assertion signature verifies over authenticatorData ||
     SHA-256(clientDataJSON), under the algorithm the stored encoding names.

  Grants: this slot, opened. No relay token, no account session, no
  authorization change (§13.9).

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. The row's question was not "Argon2id or none", and this is the third time

§13.10 keeps one role as a candidate — "an Argon2id-derived verifier" — and §15 phrases the row as
"including offline-guessing resistance". Read together they ask a work-factor question.

**They only ask it if the verifier is a function of a secret held in the profile.** Argon2id exists to make
guessing expensive; guessing is a thing you do to a secret you can check. So the question presupposes the
answer's shape, and the shape is the part worth interrogating.

**Selected: the verifier checks a signature, not a secret.** The account credential is asymmetric, the profile
holds a public key, and reopening a slot means collecting an assertion from an authenticator the profile does
not contain. Offline-guessing resistance is then not a cost imposed on the attacker but an absence: there is
nothing in the profile to grind, and "grinding" it means forging Ed25519.

**That makes three answers of _none_ to the same question, on three different arguments, and this is the
strongest of them.**

| Row | Why no stretching                                                            | Strength                                      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| 14  | The code is generated at 125 bits, so there is no entropy deficit to cover   | Unconditional, given the generation invariant |
| 13  | The same, and guessing is offline and free, so a work factor buys less still | Unconditional, and the threat is worse        |
| 12  | **There is no secret in the profile at all**                                 | Nothing to guess, so no argument to make      |

**The early-warning sign fired for the third time**, and [progress.md](../progress.md) had already named the
shape twice: row 14's "Argon2id or none" read like a selection until the entropy underneath it was designed,
and row 13's "PRF- or high-entropy-code-derived" read like one until the threat model underneath it was
written down. **Neither was the question the row appeared to ask, and neither was this.** The question here
was _what is an account credential_, which PRD:1009 defines by what it does — proves identity to the service,
leaves an offline-verifiable local slot-unlock binding — and never by what it is, while rows 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10
all bind to "credential" as a settled term.

**The embedding policy is same-origin only, and it was missing** (`S0-1`,
`f-b9ff071-webauthn-cross-origin-policy`). Step 3 read `type`, `origin` and `challenge`, and the two members
the specification adds _for the relying party to judge_ were not in the list — so an assertion collected in a
delegated iframe, with this exact origin and RP ID, verified. **The exact `origin` check does not cover it**:
in a cross-origin frame the caller is still the legitimate app origin while the top-level one differs.

**Two checks rather than one.** `topOrigin` appears only when `crossOrigin` is true, so client data carrying
`crossOrigin: false` **and** a `topOrigin` is a client contradicting itself, and a verifier reading only the
boolean accepts an embedding recorded in the bytes it just hashed. **Absent is not false** — the member is
optional and a missing one is the ordinary case — so the test is `!== true`, and the positive vectors that omit
it must still verify.

**No allowlist, because there is no embedding partner.** §10.9's boundary is this origin and row 17 forbids
third parties inside it; a list with no entries is failure modes arriving before benefits. CSP
`frame-ancestors 'none'` makes the frame unreachable and is row 17's, which leaves this the half that can be
tested from the repository. The policy lives once, in `scripts/lib/webauthn.mjs`, because row 14 §5 needs the
same one.

**And half of it was already decided, in a table nobody was reading as a selection.** §16.1's inventory row
says the authorization service stores "Account authenticator **public material** and slot-verifier parameters",
with operator visibility "None — public material". A password verifier is a server-held secret, not public
material. **The inventory foreclosed the shared-secret shape before the row was asked**, the same way row 2
had already spent the synchronous slot before row 1 noticed it had one primitive left to choose.

---

## 2. What the verifier is for, and what it cannot be for

§13.9's constraint is three clauses: proof, local, grants nothing on the network. What it does _not_ say is
which attacker it stops, and getting that wrong in either direction produces a different construction.

**It is not a confidentiality boundary against a profile holder who can execute the origin.** It cannot be.
§13.3 already scopes the default tier — "no claim against an attacker who can execute the app's origin from a
copied profile" — and `L_local` sits in that profile as a usable non-extractable handle. A gate on _reopening_
does not change what the key material can do. The construction that would change it is the device lock, and
§13.3 makes it optional and separate on purpose.

**The threat it does stop is the shared installation**, which is what D-13 and §13.9 describe in every
sentence around this one: someone signs out on a laptop, someone else sits down, and a closed slot in the
picker must not be one click from a stranger's list. That person has the profile, the origin and the keyboard.
The only thing they do not have is the authenticator.

**So the gate has to be a user-verification ceremony, and only an authenticator can supply one.** A private key
persisted in the profile — even non-extractable, even structured-cloned — proves possession of the profile,
which is exactly what the person at the keyboard already has. It would let the app satisfy its own gate
without the user doing anything, which is not a gate.

**And the offline-guessing clause protects something else again, which is why it is in §13.9 at all.** If the
verifier were a checkable function of a low-entropy secret, a profile holder could grind it offline and recover
**the account credential** — the thing that authenticates to the _service_. §13.2's row for this artifact
forbids it creating a relay session while offline; a grindable local verifier would hand over the material to
create one online. **The clause is not about the slot. It is about the verifier not becoming an offline oracle
for a network credential**, and an asymmetric credential satisfies it unconditionally.

---

## 3. Removing a secret introduces a substitutable key, and that is the load-bearing part

The verifier now reads a public key out of the slot index and checks a signature against it. **The slot index
is IndexedDB, which holds a structured clone, whose properties the load path trusts** — and row 3 already
named exactly this and gave it a rule: every cleartext field a reader trusts is authenticated.

**The attack is complete and it is one property edit.** Substitute your own passkey's public key into the
binding, assert with your own authenticator, and the slot opens. Nothing else in the record has to change.
An asymmetric verifier is not more robust than a hashed secret here — it is differently fragile, and the
fragility moves from _guessable_ to _replaceable_.

**So the binding is service-signed, and that is the construction's anchor.** The client verifies it against the
authorization key for the epoch it names, from the lineage §13.5 already has it retaining and re-verifying.
A substitution then requires the service's private key rather than write access to IndexedDB.

**This makes the gate stronger than the custody it sits beside, which is worth stating plainly because it
inverts the usual order.** `L_local` yields to anyone who can run the origin; the slot binding does not,
because the origin cannot sign as the service. The verifier resists an attacker §13.3 explicitly declines to
resist. That is a real asymmetry and it is free — §16.1's row already had the service holding these parameters
and already used the word _anchor_ for what it does with them.

**It also costs nothing new in machinery.** No new key, no new signature scheme, no new secret, no new store.
The service signs epochs already; this is one more short message under the same key, delivered at enrollment
and read offline forever after. **Row 10's move at a different object** — there, the trust root bound in every
generation wrap; here, the credential bound in a statement only the root can produce.

---

## 4. The one place the algorithm is not ours to select

Row 1's agility rule is the cleanest thing in the register: **a carrier version selects the whole suite, so
there is nothing to negotiate and nothing to downgrade.** It does not extend here, and pretending it did would
be the quiet kind of wrong.

**WebAuthn credential creation is itself a negotiation.** The relying party offers an ordered
`pubKeyCredParams`; the authenticator picks. Whatever it picks is what the credential is, for its whole life.
The project can constrain the offer and cannot choose the outcome.

**Selected: `[-8 Ed25519, -7 ES256]`, in that order, as part of the carrier version.** Ed25519 first because it
is already row 1's signature primitive, so a credential that supports it adds nothing to the suite. ES256
because it is what platform authenticators overwhelmingly produce, and because declining it would decline the
feature.

**ES256 is therefore the one primitive this row adds to §13.10's suite**, and it is added under §13.10's own
criteria rather than around them: reviewed, widely implemented, and in WebCrypto without a polyfill — so the
offline verifier needs nothing that is not already there. It is async-path only, so §13.2's separation rule is
untouched.

**RS256 is declined.** It would be a third signature primitive, in a suite selected as a whole, for a
population the first two are expected to cover.

**And row 1's property is preserved differently rather than abandoned.** The negotiation happens **once**, at
creation, and its result is frozen inside a service-signed statement. No assertion renegotiates anything;
there is no per-assertion algorithm field; a stored credential cannot change what it is. **What replaces "no
algorithm field" is "one algorithm field, signed, written once."**

**The encoding carries the algorithm, and the coverage audit is what settled that.** An earlier draft of the
signed message had `alg` as a field beside `public_key`. No negative can isolate it — the algorithm is a
function of the key encoding, so changing it alone leaves a key that verifies nothing, and changing it
consistently changes the key too — and `pnpm vectors:coverage` said so in exactly those terms: _bound in the
AAD and no negative isolates it_. **A field that cannot be varied independently is not an independent binding.**
Storing SubjectPublicKeyInfo puts the algorithm inside bytes that are already bound, and the audit went from
complaining to silent with nothing argued at it.

**Refusal, not sniffing.** The accepted encodings are a compiled-in set of two prefixes. Anything else is
refused rather than guessed at or tried against each candidate in turn — row 1's reader rule, at the one place
this design has a key type to read. The published negative is an X25519 key: valid DER, right length, wrong
job, service-signed, refused.

---

## 5. Why this role can root on the authenticator where the device lock could not

Rows 11 and 13 both concluded that a ragged capability cannot be a root, and §10.11 wrote down why: **PRF's
availability is not a browser version but a matrix of operating system, browser and authenticator kind**, with
roaming authenticators unreachable from iOS at all. Row 13 made a generated code the root and PRF an
additional seal; row 11 made QR an accelerator rather than a protocol.

**This row roots on the authenticator anyway, and the distinction is not a change of mind — it is that PRF is
an extension and a signature is not.** §10.11's own table says `webauthn` is Baseline _widely available_ since
2021-09-07 and that what it does not say is "anything about extensions". This construction uses **no WebAuthn
extension at all**: `navigator.credentials.get()` returning a signature over a challenge is the core of the
API, and the ragged part of the platform is precisely the part not used.

**There is a second reason, and it is about what the ceremony has to return.** The device lock needs _key
material_ — something to seal `L_lock` under — and only PRF produces that. This row needs a _proof_, and a
proof is checkable against a public key. **A signature is checkable offline without being guessable offline;
a derived key is not.** That sentence is the whole difference between the two rows, and it is why they reach
opposite conclusions from the same threat model.

**One consequence for row 13's vectors, and it is a correction rather than an addition.** Row 13's separation
vectors reserve a PRF evaluation label for this role — `done/slot-verifier-prf/v1` — as one of §13.4's four
factor roles, marked a provisional stand-in owned by a 3b row. **This row uses no PRF, so one of §13.4's four
factor roles turns out not to consume a factor output at all.** §13.4's requirement that the four be
domain-separated and never substituted is satisfied structurally here: there is no output to separate. Row
13's file is amended to say so — the label stays reserved and is now recorded as unused, which is a changed
comment string in a generated file and no changed vector value. **Row 11's amendment one commit after
selection is the precedent**, and the reason is the same: nothing has been built, so a correction costs a
regenerated file today and a protocol version after the first deployment.

**What is still asserted rather than verified: that an authenticator is present.** §10.11's floor answers the
API and cannot answer this, because presence is a runtime condition rather than a version — the same shape as
PRF, one step less ragged. **What happens when it is absent is stated rather than left open** (§7), and the
runtime check is `PublicKeyCredential.isUserVerifyingPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable()`.

---

## 6. The challenge, and the cross-protocol edge it exists for

**The same credential authenticates to the service.** So an assertion is a proof that two different verifiers
read, and the interesting direction is the one that looks safe: **a slot-unlock assertion presented to the
service as a sign-in.** §13.2's row forbids this artifact creating a relay session while offline, and an
assertion that is indistinguishable from a sign-in is how that rule gets broken by an implementation that
never decided to break it.

**Two conditions refuse it, and both are stated because the client can only check one.** The purpose is inside
the challenge preimage, as the domain-separation label; and the service's own challenges are service-issued
and single-use, so a client-minted challenge is not one it ever issued. The second is a service behaviour and
therefore 3b's to confirm rather than this document's to assert.

**Bound, not fresh.** Row 14 §5 rejected a freshness window for step-up on the grounds that the thing it
approximates is _this assertion was collected for this operation_ — so bind that directly. The same rule
applies here and costs the same nothing: no clock, no skew, nothing to tune on a device whose clock is wrong.
The challenge binds the slot and the credential; a nonce makes it unrepeatable.

**The binding's fields are deliberately not hashed into the challenge wholesale.** A single `binding_digest`
field would be a function of all eight bound fields, so any negative isolating it would also be isolated by
whichever of those eight it varied — two fields for one negative, which the coverage audit refuses and is
right to. Naming the two fields the challenge actually needs is both cheaper and testable.

**And the challenge negatives are not enough on their own, which is row 9's lesson arriving a second time.**
They fail on a string comparison between the challenge carried and the challenge expected — **which fails
whether or not the signature covers the challenge at all.** The isolating negative rewrites `clientDataJSON`
to carry the expected value, so the comparison passes and only the signature can refuse it. That is also the
real attack, since `clientDataJSON` arrives from the same place the assertion does.

---

## 7. Where the guarantee stops

Three bounds, named here rather than left for a reviewer to find. None of them is closed by anything this row
could add.

**A binding outlives a revocation this device has not seen.** It is signed in an epoch; a device that has been
closed since then has not seen the epoch that revoked the credential, and the binding still verifies. **§13.9
is what bounds it**: reopening grants no relay token, no account session and no authorization change, so what a
stale binding opens is already-local state and nothing else. §13.5's lineage closes it the moment the device is
online. D-13 already wrote the same sentence for a deleted account — "the retained local verifier may still
reopen the slot offline; it cannot restore the deleted service relationship" — and this is that sentence one
level down. It is published as a demonstration rather than a negative, because it succeeds.

**Deleting a binding is not prevented, and does not need to be.** Whoever can edit the slot index can remove an
unlock path; they cannot add one. That is availability, and it is strictly less than deleting the index
outright, which the same access already permits.

**Sign-out plus a lost authenticator plus no network is an availability failure, and the product owes copy for
it.** The data is not lost — it is sealed, local and intact — but the ordinary gate cannot be satisfied until
the service is reachable and a replacement credential is enrolled. D-13 names the offline fallback for the
harder case: importing the terminal package and presenting the recovery factor. **That does not contradict
§13.3's rule that recovery may not open a locked slot**, and the distinction is worth keeping straight: §13.9
has two independent gates, the account-credential proof and the optional device-lock factor. Recovery is a
fallback for the first. The second still has to be satisfied, and row 13's prohibition is untouched.

**A device with no authenticator has no local verifier at all**, and §13.9 already contains the honest
sentence for it, with a different subject: "A purely accountless Local slot has no account credential, so the
product does not present account sign-out as though it could protect it. Its honest handoff on a shared
installation is export then reset." **The degradation was already written; it needed a second subject rather
than a new mechanism.**

---

## 8. What it costs

| Cost                 | Measured or bounded                                              | Against                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bundle               | **None new**                                                     | Ed25519 and ECDSA P-256 verification are WebCrypto; WebAuthn is a browser API. No stretching library, which is what the Argon2id candidate would have cost |
| Suite                | **One primitive added** — ES256, async path only                 | §13.10's criteria, met; §13.2's separation rule, untouched                                                                                                 |
| Slot index size      | ~150 bytes per credential                                        | Per slot, for a handful of credentials                                                                                                                     |
| Reopen latency       | One assertion ceremony, one Ed25519 verify, one assertion verify | Off §12's budget: a local unlock precedes cold start as a ceremony, on row 13's reasoning                                                                  |
| Service work         | One short signature at enrollment                                | The same key that signs epochs                                                                                                                             |
| Codes the user files | **None.** This is not a fourth code                              | Rows 13 and 14's two, unchanged                                                                                                                            |

## 9. Which review holds it — answered, and the answer is that it stays in 3b

[progress.md](../progress.md) has carried an open question with two rows pointing at it: the slot verifier
looks storage-shaped, §13.9 names it and the device lock in one sentence, and 3a is the engagement with the
context — so 3b would be reviewing a construction whose reasoning lives in a document its reviewer has not
read. Row 13 sharpened it and declined to settle it, correctly, since reassignment is a change to §15.

**It is settled by the construction rather than by a judgement call, and it stays in 3b.** The row looked
storage-shaped because _offline-guessing resistance_ implied a secret at rest, and a secret at rest is §6's
business. There is no secret at rest. What is left is an account credential, a service signature, an epoch, a
challenge and a cross-protocol replay boundary — all of it network-facing, all of it 3b's, and none of it
resting on §13.3's threat model except by contrast (§5).

**So 3a's closed scope stays closed**, which is the outcome worth having with the review three working days
out. The seam progress.md flagged is closed by being answered rather than by being moved.

---

## 10. What Stage 4 owes, and what is still open

**Owed by Stage 4, and none of it is Stage 1's.** Nothing in this row touches the on-disk shape: the slot index
gains a field at the point Stage 4 creates accounts, and until then there are no accounts and no bindings.

- **The `pubKeyCredParams` offer is a compiled-in constant**, and the conformance test that turns §4's
  algorithm claim into a check belongs to §11.2 with the rest of Stage 4's, exactly as row 1's Ed25519
  availability did.
- **Enrollment writes a binding per credential**, and the ordering rule is the one row 13 found for its own
  enrollment: the state that must never exist is a slot with a closed flag and no binding.
- **The copy for sign-out** has to say what it will ask for on the way back in, because §7's third bound is
  only tolerable if the person met it before they chose it rather than after.

**Open, and offered to 3b rather than answered here.**

- **Whether an authenticator's presence deserves a floor statement in §10.11.** §5 argues it cannot be a
  version and therefore cannot be a floor, which is PRF's answer at less severity — but PRF got that treatment
  because a row asked for it, and this row is asserting it. The evidence to take is which current-stable
  platform-and-browser combinations expose a user-verifying authenticator, and it is the same kind of
  measurement §10.11 already carries dates for.
- **Whether the service rate-limits assertion verification, and its challenge-issuance semantics.** Row 14 §5
  hands 3b two service behaviours already; §6's second refusal condition is a third, and they are one
  question about what the account service promises.
- **Account-credential recovery is deliberately not specified here**, and §13.8's four-object table is why it
  can be ordinary: account access is object 1, supplied by account recovery, and no mechanism supplies
  another's. **The thing that makes a boring account-recovery flow safe is the same separation that makes the
  recovery code mandatory** — email can restore an account and can never restore a content key. Saying so is
  worth more than specifying a flow this row does not own.

---

## 11. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-account-credential-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale. The
generator verifies itself on every run: both keypairs are checked half against half, every published vector is
run through the real verifier, every negative is asserted to fail, and the published must-fail list is
compared against what was actually asserted in both directions.

**Three kinds, and one of them succeeds on purpose.**

The **binding vectors** pin the signed message and its signature, for both accepted key encodings. They are the
row's whole claim in eight length-prefixed fields.

The **assertion vectors** pin the challenge preimage, the authenticator data, the client data and the bytes the
credential actually signs. **The Ed25519 one is pinned to its signature and the ES256 one is not**, and the
asymmetry is deliberate: Ed25519 is deterministic, so its signature is a fact about the construction, while
ECDSA's is randomized and publishing one would pin **this generator's RNG** rather than anything specified. The
ES256 vector carries every byte that is specified and mints a signature at generation time to verify.

The **demonstrations** are behaviours that succeed and are meant to, which row 6 established as the honest way
to publish a residual. `sign-count-is-read-and-ignored` is the one an implementer needs: WebAuthn's counter
exists to detect a cloned authenticator, a synced passkey cannot maintain one and reports zero forever, and a
verifier enforcing monotonicity **refuses the ordinary case while detecting nothing.** It is stated here so the
omission does not read as an oversight.

The **negatives**, twenty-two, in three groups.

The _anchor_ group is the attack the construction exists for. `forged-binding-under-other-key` performs it
competently — the attacker's key in the record, the attacker's assertion, and the binding re-signed so the
record is internally consistent — and it fails on the one thing in the profile a profile holder cannot produce.

The _ceremony_ group is what the verifier checks about the assertion itself: an unbound credential, a UP-only
assertion, another relying party, another origin, a registration ceremony presented as an assertion, a flipped
bit, and `challenge-rewritten-to-match`.

The _field_ group is the coverage rule: thirteen fields across two bound lists, each isolated by a negative that
changes it and nothing else. **The first pass had fourteen, and three of them refused for the same reason —
`rp_id`, `alg` and `public_key` are read by the verifier as well as bound in the signed message, so the obvious
negative fails twice and proves neither.** `rp_id` and `public_key` are fixed by supplying a _consistent_
ceremony for the substituted value, so only the binding can refuse it — which is also what the real attacker
would do. **`alg` is not fixed, because it cannot be**, and that is how it stopped being the fourteenth (§4). **Row 9's finding, that the audit
catches the thing the row was built for, held here too** — `aad-only-binding-public-key` is the negative this
entire document exists to justify, and its first version was passing for the wrong reason.
